rows.question: Can a CUDA event that has never been recorded establish successful completion of earlier work? Explain precisely.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Can a CUDA event that has never been recorded establish successful completion of earlier work? Explain precisely.
rows.answer: No. A CUDA event that has never been recorded can report success, but that does not establish completion of earlier work. Before its first recording, cudaEventQuery and cudaEventSynchronize return cudaSuccess because the event represents an empty set of work—not because they checked preceding GPU operations. To establish completion, record the event after the relevant work in its stream, then successfully query or synchronize that recording; work in other streams requires explicit dependencies.

review.note: Never-recorded event success denotes empty work; record after relevant stream operations and qualify unrelated streams.
review.usefulPrefix: No. A CUDA event that has never been recorded can report success, but that does not establish completion of earlier work.

rows.name: context-15
rows.question: A client retries a charge operation after a network timeout. How does a durable idempotency key avoid a duplicate charge, and what must be atomic?
rows.recognizedQuestion: A client retries a charge operation after a network timeout. How does a durable idempotency key avoid a duplicate charge, and what must be atomic?
rows.answer: The client reuses the same idempotency key, and the server durably associates that key with one charge and its result, so a retry returns the existing result rather than charging again. Claiming the key must be atomic against concurrent requests, and the charge’s committed effect must be atomically linked to the stored idempotency outcome—otherwise a crash between charging and saving the result can cause a duplicate. If an external payment provider performs the charge, use the same stable key with its idempotency mechanism and reconcile uncertain outcomes; a local database transaction alone cannot make the external charge atomic.

review.note: Durable idempotent outcome/charge atomicity, concurrent claim and external-provider boundary/reconciliation.
review.usefulPrefix: The client reuses the same idempotency key, and the server durably associates that key with one charge and its result, so a retry returns the existing result rather than charging again.

rows.name: context-16
rows.question: Why?
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why?
rows.answer: Because a timeout means the client doesn’t know whether the charge succeeded—not that it failed. Atomically claiming the key prevents concurrent retries from creating separate charges, and atomically committing the charge with its durable outcome prevents a crash from leaving a completed charge without a record. If an external provider performs the charge, it must also deduplicate retries using the same stable key; a local database transaction alone cannot make the external charge atomic.

review.note: Timeout may hide success; charge/dedup atomicity and stable provider key explain retry safety.
review.usefulPrefix: Because a timeout means the client doesn’t know whether the charge succeeded—not that it failed.

rows.name: context-28
rows.question: Actually switch to database isolation. Explain the difference between snapshot isolation and serializability with a concrete write-skew example.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Actually switch to database isolation. Explain the difference between snapshot isolation and serializability with a concrete write-skew example.
rows.answer:
Snapshot isolation gives each transaction a consistent snapshot, but serializability guarantees an outcome equivalent to running transactions one at a time. Snapshot isolation can allow write skew when transactions update different rows based on the same stale snapshot.

For example, Alice and Bob are both on call, and at least one must remain on call. Two concurrent transactions each read that both are on call: one takes Alice off call, while the other takes Bob off call. Under snapshot isolation, both can commit because they update different rows, leaving nobody on call.

That outcome is not serializable: whichever transaction ran second would see only one doctor still on call and refuse to remove them. Serializable isolation prevents both transactions from committing that outcome, typically by blocking or aborting one; an aborted transaction must retry and recheck the rule.

review.note: Concrete two-doctor disjoint-row snapshot write skew violates invariant; serializable equivalent order prevents both off.
review.usefulPrefix: Snapshot isolation gives each transaction a consistent snapshot, but serializability guarantees an outcome equivalent to running transactions one at a time.

rows.name: context-29
rows.question: Correction: use a single atomic transaction for the entire read-check-write invariant. Does that alone guarantee serializability under snapshot isolation?
rows.recognizedQuestion: Correction: use a single atomic transaction for the entire read-check-write invariant. Does that alone guarantee serializability under snapshot isolation?
rows.answer: No. Making the entire read-check-write operation one atomic transaction does not make snapshot isolation serializable. Alice’s and Bob’s transactions can each read a snapshot showing both on call, check that someone else remains, and update their own separate row; both can commit, leaving nobody on call. In either serial execution, the second transaction would see only one person on call and refuse that update, so this outcome is not serializable. Preventing it requires serializable isolation or explicit coordination that forces these transactions to conflict.

review.note: Whole read-check-write transaction atomicity alone does not protect cross-row invariant under SI.
review.usefulPrefix: No. Making the entire read-check-write operation one atomic transaction does not make snapshot isolation serializable.

rows.recognizedQuestion: Why?
rows.answer: Atomicity guarantees all-or-nothing execution, not that concurrent transactions behave as if run one at a time. Under snapshot isolation, both transactions can read Alice and Bob as on call, pass the check, and each switch a different person off; because they write different rows, both can commit. In either serial order, the second transaction would see just one person on call and refuse to switch them off, so the concurrent outcome is not serializable.

review.note: Causal all-or-nothing versus serial order explanation; concrete snapshots/both off incompatible with either serial order.
review.usefulPrefix: Atomicity guarantees all-or-nothing execution, not that concurrent transactions behave as if run one at a time.
